Timed comments that cross the video as clickable DOM

Each comment below is an HTML element that the canvas draws over the video, at a position worked out from the time of the video frame. Press Play. Tap a comment to stop it and open its Like button. Write one of your own and it's added at the current time.

Show the code comments as cues, one element each, placed per frame
  1. The markup. The video and a control bar are children of the canvas. Comment elements are added beside them.
  2. Store comments as cues. video.addTextTrack('metadata') makes a track that is never shown. Each comment is a VTTCue whose text is JSON.
  3. One element per active cue. The same library as the captions page, with a render function that makes a comment.
  4. The comment element. A drawable div holding buttons.
  5. Where a comment is at a time. A function of the media time, so the same time always gives the same picture.
  6. Draw. One drawElementImage() call per comment, inside a transform. The call also moves the element's hit-test region.
  7. Taps. Ordinary click handlers on the buttons.
  8. Export. exportFrames() seeks the video frame by frame, and onframe chooses the comments for each time.
  9. The CSS.

How it works

  • The comments live in a text track of kind metadata. A cue runs from the comment's time for 4 seconds, the time a comment takes to cross. The browser keeps activeCues current, so the page holds elements only for the comments on screen.
  • Every comment is its own drawable child of the canvas. The paint handler computes x = W − (t − start) ÷ 4 × (W + width) from the media time t that requestVideoFrameCallback() reported for the frame, and draws the element there.
  • drawElementImage() sets the element's hit-test region to where it was drawn, including the rotation in the wave mode. A tap on a moving comment is an ordinary click on its button.
  • The inverting mode sets globalCompositeOperation = 'difference' for the draw call. White text then shows the inverse of the frame under it.
  • A Like is written back into the cue's JSON text, so the count is still there when the video loops and the element is built again.
  • The export pauses the video, seeks to each frame time and asks the cue library for the cues at that time by comparing times, because activeCues is updated only after the seek has finished.

ResultExperimentDetail

Findings

From Chromium 157 headless with software video decoding, 2026-11-21. The rows above say what your browser does.

  • Works: a metadata track as the store. addTextTrack('metadata') starts in the hidden mode, and cues added by script enter activeCues like cues from a file.
  • Works: elements added and removed while the video plays. A new drawable child can't be drawn until the browser has recorded it once. The first drawElementImage() call throws, so the paint handler skips the element and asks for another paint.
  • Works: the position matches the frame. The third check plays a fixture and, in each paint, reads the frame number from the stripes in the picture. It reports how many paints drew the comment for that same frame.
  • Works: taps on moving and rotated comments. elementFromPoint() finds the comment's button at the drawn place, and no longer finds it there after the comment has moved on.
  • Works: the difference blend mode on an element. The composite operation applies to drawElementImage() as it does to drawImage().
  • Works: frame-exact export. In an exported file the comment moves the same number of pixels in every frame.
  • Limit: a comment that starts in the last 4 seconds is cut off when the clip loops. Its cue can't run past the end of the video.
  • Not verified: the frame match with a hardware decoder on Android, the cost of 30 or more comments on a phone, and tapping a moving comment with a finger. The third check and the line under the player report the first two on the device.
